RICHARD WHITING | INDEX-JOURNAL Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Breaking Ascend to close Greenwood County plant in February By RICHARD WHITING rwhiting@indexjournal.com Oct 16, 2024 Oct 16, 2024 Updated Nov 22, 2025 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Buy Now Ascend Performance Materials in Greenwood County announced Wednesday it will close its plant by February 2025, affecting about 200 employees. The plant entrance is at the intersection of Highway 246 and Emerald Road. RICHARD WHITING | INDEX-JOURNAL Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Ascend Performance Materials today announced it is closing its plant in Greenwood County early next year, citing global economic issues. The closure will affect about 200 employees. “Our employees in Greenwood brought hard work and dedication to every aspect of their work,” Phil McDivitt, president and CEO, said in a press release sent from its Houston headquarters. “Ultimately, prolonged global economic pressure, especially in the automotive and construction sectors, led to the difficult decision to close the plant,” McDivitt said. Ascend’s Greenwood County plant, situated off Highway 246 and operating near other industries, including Fujifilm’s remaining operations, Enviva’s wood pellet plant and Teijin’s carbon fiber plant, manufactures nylon polymer and fiber used to create airbags, carpet and textiles. The company will exit fiber production and shift its polymer operations to its Cantonment plant in Pensacola, Florida. The Pensacola plant, however, on Oct. 10 announced it is laying off employees but not shutting down completely, according to a news report on NorthEscambia.com . The news site cited Osama Khalifa, Ascend director of corporate communications and government affairs, as its source of information. “The company did not disclose the number of layoffs at the plant over the past few months, or address if there would be additional layoffs,” the news site reported. According to data from economic development authority FloridaWest, Ascend was the sixth largest employer in Escambia County, with 1,288 employees, NorthEscambia.com reported. The closure of Greenwood County’s plant directly affects about 200 employees, Khalifa said in a statement sent Wednesday evening to the Index-Journal. Khalifa said the company is providing resources to assist employees with new-skill training, financial planning and job search assistance. The company is also working with other area businesses to hold on-site job fairs. “I want to thank the employees at our Greenwood plant for their years of dedicated service,” Michael Walters, Ascend’s senior site director in the Greenwood County plant. “Despite the circumstances, they have a lot to be proud of and we are focusing our efforts on smoothing this transition for them.” Ascend’s website says the Greenwood County plant makes materials for “everyday essentials and new technologies.” Based in Houston, Texas, and with regional offices in Shanghai, Brussels and Detroit, Ascend has global manufacturing facilities in North America, Europe and Asia. Shifts made in January On Jan. 16, Ascend announced plans to close its industrial fiber spinning operation in the Greenwood County plant and its engineered materials compounding site in Tilburg, Netherlands. ( https://shorturl.at/ORdE1 ) The company said then that the Greenwood County facility “will continue to produce staple fiber, bulked continuous filament and specialty polymers.” “The teams in Tilburg and Greenwood have worked safely and diligently in the face of ongoing and unprecedented economic challenges for nearly two years,” McDivitt said in the January announcement. “We made these difficult, but necessary decisions to better serve our customers long-term.” Whiting is executive editor of the Index-Journal. Nylon maker Ascend files for bankruptcy Share Save News Finance Nylon maker Ascend files for bankruptcy The firm was overcome by debt and a tough market by Alexander Tullo April 24, 2025 3 min read Share Save Save News The latest chemistry news, including important research advances, business and policy trends, chemical safety practices, career guidance, and more. Read More Ascend Performance Materials produces nylon 6,6 at this facility in Pensacola, Florida. Credit: Ascend Performance Materials Struggling with debt and a market swamped with overcapacity, the nylon 6,6 producer Ascend Performance Materials has declared bankruptcy in Texas. Ascend says that it is pursuing an easy restructuring process that will wrap up in about 6 months. It has secured $250 million in debtor-in-possession financing that will allow it to continue running its operations in the interim. Headquartered in Houston and with its manufacturing primarily in the US, Ascend makes nylon 6,6 and its precursors, acrylonitrile, adiponitrile, adipic acid, and hexamethylenediamine (HMD). The company had sales of $2.4 billion in 2023. The New York City–based private equity firm SK Capital bought the business, which had been losing money, from Solutia in 2009 for the bargain price of $50 million in cash. Under SK’s ownership, Ascend has expanded production, most notably building an HMD plant in China that it completed last year. Ascend bought a majority stake in the plastics recycler Circular Polymers in 2022. Ascend blames the bankruptcy on its underlying financial structure and high debt obligations. "Over the last several months, we have been working with our lenders to define the best path forward,” Ascend CEO Phil McDivitt says in an announcement. The firm took out a $1.1 billion loan in 2019, which the credit rating agency S&P Global Ratings said at the time was to refinance debt and fund a special dividend to shareholders. This past February, S&P downgraded its rating for Ascend because of underperformance in 2024 and a “challenging operating environment.” Last year, Ascend closed its compounding plant in Tilburg, the Netherlands. Earlier this year, the company closed a facility in Greenwood, South Carolina, where it made nylon polymer and fiber. “Globally, nylon 6,6 is experiencing oversupply across the entire value chain driven by overexpansion in mainland China,” says Meiko Woo, an executive director at the market research firm Chemical Market Analytics by OPIS. “The US is the largest nylon 6,6 exporter, with the majority of volumes going to Asia and Europe,” Woo says. “The growing presence of mainland China in the rest of Asia is pressuring US nylon 6,6 production.” Ascend’s chief US rival, Invista, put its nylon fiber business up for sale last year but decided earlier this month to keep it after engaging in a marketing process for the unit. In addition, US exports to Europe have slowed because of a weakened economy there. European competitors to Ascend, such as BASF and Domo Chemicals, have also announced that they are closing nylon 6,6–related assets. Nylon 6,6 producers in the US also face competition from lower-priced alternatives such as nylon 6, polyester, and imports of finished goods that contain nylon. “As a result, the nylon 6,6 industry in the US is grappling with subdued demand and compressed margins,” Woo says. close compounding site, industrial fibers production January 16, 2024 Ascend Performance Materials has announced plans to close its engineered materials compounding site in Tilburg, Netherlands and its industrial fiber spinning operation in Greenwood, South Carolina.  In Europe and pending agreement with the relevant bodies, Ascend intends to transfer its Vydyne® production from Tilburg to Mozzate, Italy in April. The facility in Mozzate houses state-of-the-art equipment, a recycling R&D center and in-house masterbatch production.  For industrial fibers, shipments will cease in early Q2 2024. Ascend will continue supplying high-quality polymer to the industrial fiber industry. The site in Greenwood will continue to produce staple fiber, bulked continuous filament and specialty polymers.  “The teams in Tilburg and Greenwood have worked safely and diligently in the face of ongoing and unprecedented economic challenges for nearly two years,” said Phil McDivitt, Ascend’s president and CEO. “We made these difficult, but necessary decisions to better serve our customers long-term.”  More news Safety Leadership: The ESSH Excellence Award April 29, 2026 Ascend cuts ribbon on new high-purity acetonitrile production February 4, 2026 Ascend Performance Materials Successfully Emerges from Chapter 11 December 19, 2025 Newsroom Insights Press Releases Life at Ascend Newsletter Sign up to receive our latest news and information about upcoming events Email * Privacy and consent terms + - Ascend is committed to protecting and respecting your privacy, and we’ll only use your personal information to administer your account and to provide the products and services you requested from us.
